naming_quality.issues_preventing_higher_score: should_* helpers returning dicts, mixed to_dict/as_dict serialization names, and mixed lm_studio/lmstudio spellings create recurring 'which name do I use?' friction.

cross_module_architecture.dimension_character: The codebase has a conventional layered shape (domain, services, API, CLI) with stable domain and configuration hubs, but recurring boundary leaks invert service-to-API dependencies, expose private helpers across modules, and coordinate state through mutable globals. These issues are concentrated in the largest orchestration modules rather than spread uniformly.
cross_module_architecture.score_rationale: A developer can generally predict dependency direction and follow the main layers, which keeps the score above the mixed range. However, inverted service-to-API imports, shared mutable run state, cross-module private helper use, an import cycle, and heavy deferred-import pressure create real coupling hotspots that make changes ripple unexpectedly in the optimizer, routes, and CLI modules.

high_level_elegance.dimension_character: The project has a broadly capability-oriented package layout (backends, benchmark, hardware, profiles, storage), but ownership is blurred by a duplicate LM Studio client, a deprecated engine still wired into active paths, a 65-module flat services catch-all, and stale version/test-count contracts. Public surfaces and entry points are therefore less predictable than the directory tree initially suggests.
high_level_elegance.score_rationale: Core decomposition is serviceable and many subpackages map to real capabilities, which prevents a low score. However, duplicate clients, legacy shims, monolithic service/CLI modules, mixed api/ roles, and documentation drift materially weaken top-level ownership clarity, supporting a mid-60s score.

convention_outlier.dimension_character: The codebase is broadly consistent in low-level naming (snake_case everywhere, dataclass domain models), but several major capabilities are implemented twice under the same class names in different layers, and file/module naming drifts for the same product (LM Studio). A developer can trust small-scale conventions but cannot trust that a class name or module path identifies a single implementation.
convention_outlier.score_rationale: Strong baseline consistency in naming and type strategy keeps the score above the 60 anchor, but recurring parallel implementations (LMStudioClient, QualityEvaluator, OptimizationState) and incomplete package migrations create the 'why is this different?' friction described by the 80 anchor. The drift is concentrated in client and optimizer layers rather than spread across every module, so the score sits in the mid-70s.

error_consistency.dimension_character: Error handling is reasonably structured in newer services, with typed errors and Result objects, but older and boundary code still mixes swallowed exceptions, bool/None returns, and inconsistent propagation. A developer can usually tell whether an operation failed, but not always why or how the failure will surface. The strongest patterns are in defaults and host-guard code; the weakest are in API listing and best-effort CLI/report helpers.
error_consistency.score_rationale: The codebase avoids total unpredictability by using typed errors and Result types in important paths, which supports a score above 60. However, recurring silent swallowing and mixed return strategies across related modules create the recurring 'why is this different?' friction described by the 80 anchor's lower bound, keeping the score in the low 70s. The issues are concentrated but not isolated to one file.

naming_quality.dimension_character: Overall naming is clear and convention-driven: snake_case is used consistently, most predicates return bool, and domain terms are descriptive. The rough edges are concentrated in a few vocabulary splits (to_dict vs as_dict, lm_studio vs lmstudio) and predicate names that promise a boolean but return a recommendation dict.
naming_quality.score_rationale: The codebase mostly serves a developer well on naming (anchor ~90), but the mixed serialization spellings and product-name spellings plus two misleading should_* names are recurring enough to push it down to the mid-80s. None of the issues are pervasive or obscure core logic, which keeps the score above 80.

add.header: Layered package layout with domain services API CLI
add.description: Production code is organized into recognizable domain, services, API, and CLI layers, with domain models acting as the shared vocabulary.

add.header: BackendClient protocol seam with conformance tests
add.description: Backend clients are checked against a documented BackendClient protocol, including LM Studio and Ollama implementations.

add.header: Deprecated legacy modules are explicitly marked
add.description: Legacy optimizer and web UI modules state their deprecated status and point to authoritative replacements.

add.header: API routes module owns in-memory job state
add.description: Run, compare, sandbox, and judge job state is held in module-level dictionaries in api/routes.py and accessed by other API modules.

add.header: Deferred imports signal cycle pressure in monoliths
add.description: Routes, CLI, optimizer, and lab modules use dozens of function-level imports to work around import cycles.
lm_optimizer uses focused subpackages for backends, benchmark, hardware, profiles, storage, and ui, which gives new engineers a mostly predictable ownership map.
The services package has grown to 65 modules without subpackages, so domain ownership and change boundaries are increasingly implicit.
Deprecated optimizer and web UI modules are retained for compatibility but still imported by active paths, blurring which implementation is authoritative.
All functions, classes-adjacent helpers and module files use snake_case consistently across the Python codebase.
Domain objects consistently use dataclass or frozen dataclass rather than a mix of TypedDict, NamedTuple and dataclass strategies.
Several capabilities exist in both a legacy module and a newer seam-conforming module under identical class names, creating convention drift.
Service filenames alternate between lm_studio_ and lmstudio_ prefixes (plus lms_), so the product name has no single canonical module spelling.

add.header: Typed defaults errors with cause chaining
add.description: lmstudio_defaults and ollama_defaults share a DefaultsError hierarchy and preserve causes with 'from e', giving predictable failure modes for defaults operations.
Many I/O and cleanup paths catch broad exceptions and degrade to empty/False results; some log, but several silently pass, making failures hard to trace.
Production modules and functions consistently use snake_case, with PascalCase reserved for classes; no camelCase leakage observed.
Most is_/has_/can_/should_ predicates return bool, so callers can use them directly in conditions; only two should_* helpers are exceptions.
Classes use both to_dict and as_dict for the same conversion, so callers must remember which spelling each type uses.
Module and identifier names alternate between lm_studio and lmstudio for the same product, fragmenting search and imports.
